desc:
A round cake is cut into m slices in circular order; slice i has size slices[i], and slice m - 1 is a neighbour of slice 0. You must take exactly k slices and no two taken slices may be neighbours on the circle.

Return the largest total size you can take. The input always allows a valid choice.

For example, for slices = [8, 9, 8, 6, 1, 1] the answer is 16 when k = 2 (the two 8s at indices 0 and 2) and 17 when k = 3 (indices 0, 2 and 4: 8 + 8 + 1).
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ floor(slices.length / 2), so a valid choice always exists
hints: Remove the circle first: if the slices were in a straight line, how would you pick exactly k non-adjacent ones with maximum sum?
In the circle, slices 0 and m-1 are neighbours, so any valid choice leaves out slice 0 or slice m-1 (or both).
Run the exactly-k line DP f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i-2][j-1] + a[i-1]) on slices[0..m-2] and on slices[1..m-1], then return the larger f[.][k].
editorial: On a straight line the problem is solved by the DP f[i][j] = max(f[i-1][j], f[i-2][j-1] + a[i-1]) where j is the number of slices taken, with f[i][0] = 0 and unreachable states marked as very negative. The circle adds just one constraint: slices 0 and m-1 are neighbours, so they cannot both be taken.

Hence every valid choice avoids slice 0 or avoids slice m-1. The best choice avoiding the last slice is the line answer on slices[0..m-2]; the best one avoiding the first is the line answer on slices[1..m-1]. Return the larger of the two. For k ≤ floor(m / 2) both lines contain a valid selection (a line of m-1 elements holds up to floor(m / 2) non-adjacent picks). Time O(m · k), space O(k). This is the circular trick of House Robber II combined with a pick counter.
